definition.text: A tax, proposed by Swedish economist Erik Lindahl, in which each person pays for a public good according to the extra benefit they get from one more unit of it.

facts.text: Lindahl put forward the idea in 1919, influenced by his teacher Knut Wicksell, to show that agreement on public spending is possible.
If each person's tax price equals their own marginal benefit at the ideal level, everyone is better off and may agree to that level of provision.
In a worked example, a park costs $15 per acre; Sarah and Tom together will pay $15 at the 60th acre, so Sarah pays $5 and Tom $10 for each of 60 acres.
In theory it provides public goods efficiently, but it needs each person's demand, which is hard to know in practice.
People may understate their benefits to pay less, may not know their own valuation (for national defense, say), and government may struggle to add valuations up.

definition.text: The problem of finding out how much the public really wants a public good, when there is no market to make people show what it is worth to them.

facts.text: Without full knowledge of people's preferences, government planners are likely to supply too much or too little of a public good.
Since only individuals know their own benefit, they have a reason to understate it, a form of free riding.
Mechanisms such as Vickrey-Clarke-Groves aim to draw out true values, but none has fully solved the problem, and asking a large population is costly in money and time.

title: New institutional economics

definition.text: A school of economics that studies the institutions, meaning the legal rules and social norms, that underlie economic activity.

facts.text: It assumes people are rational but have limited minds and information and find agreements hard to enforce, so institutions arise largely to cut transaction costs.
It grew from Ronald Coase's papers 'The Nature of the Firm' (1937) and 'The Problem of Social Cost' (1960); Oliver Williamson coined the name in 1975.
Following Douglass North, institutions are 'the rules of the game', formal laws and informal norms, while organizations are the teams that play.
Associated Nobel laureates include Daron Acemoglu, Ronald Coase, Douglass North, Elinor Ostrom and Oliver Williamson.
Critics say it overlooks the coercion and power politics involved in creating and keeping institutions.

related: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

conflicts.text: In 1972 Harold Demsetz and Armen Alchian published the work described as founding New Institutional Economics.
conflicts.note: The NIE page dates the name to Williamson in 1975; this is a founding claim rather than the coining, so not strictly the same quantity.

definition.text: A useful good that its owner can keep others from using and that one person's use uses up for others.

facts.text: Bread is a private good: a loaf one person eats cannot be eaten by another, and a baker can refuse to sell it.
Private goods are scarce, which can create competition for them.
Unlike public goods such as clean air, private goods rarely suffer from free riding.
Market demand for a private good is found by adding up how much each person will buy at each price (horizontal summation), unlike public goods, whose individual demands are summed vertically.

title: Private property

definition.text: Ownership of property by people or organizations other than the government.

facts.text: It differs from public property, owned by the state, and from collective or cooperative property.
Private property is a legal idea defined and enforced by each country's legal and political institutions, and it is the foundation of capitalism.
John Locke's chief argument for owning land privately was that it led to better land management and farming than common land.
Supporters say private ownership puts land to productive use, protects its value, and lets it be traded or used as collateral.
Owners' rights usually come with limits, such as building codes or bans on demolishing historic buildings.
Socialists criticize private ownership of the means of production, and critics also call property law a tool of empire that ignored Indigenous common ownership of land.

contested_note: Economic liberals see private property as essential to prosperity, while socialists and other critics see it as a source of exploitation, inequality and land appropriation.
